name: Coda-Pelagic
geological_features: Shallow global ocean averaging only 3 kilometers deep
Vast coral-analogue reef systems visible from orbit
Submerged karst topography creating underwater cave networks
specific_features: The Final Reef — an unbroken ring of coral-analogue encircling the equator
Seasonal ice formation at the poles that calves into musical floating sculptures
resources: Calcium carbonate deposits of architectural quality
Clean freshwater ice from polar calving
description: Coda-Pelagic is a small, cool oceanic world with a remarkably shallow global ocean. The water is crystal clear in most regions, allowing the spectacular reef systems below to be visible from considerable altitude. The equatorial Final Reef is the planet's most striking feature — an unbroken ring of living coral-analogue that girdles the entire world.

The low gravity gives the ocean an almost ethereal quality, with waves that rise slowly and fall gently, and spray that hangs in the air like mist. The atmosphere is clean and cold, carrying the sharp salt-mineral scent of the reef. At the poles, seasonal ice formations calve into the ocean as delicate, translucent sculptures that drift equatorward, chiming softly as they melt.

Coda-Pelagic appears to be a world in its final biological epoch. The reef systems, while currently thriving, show geological evidence of steady decline over millions of years, each generation building on the bones of the last but reaching slightly less high. The ocean itself is slowly evaporating into space due to the weak gravity, a process that will leave the planet dry within a hundred million years.

The planet's beauty has made it a destination for contemplative tourism, and a small but devoted community of artists and philosophers has established floating habitats among the ice sculptures. Scientists study the reef ecology as a model for understanding long-term biosphere decline, while preservationists debate whether intervention to halt the ocean loss would be an act of mercy or hubris.
